q: Redis answers in about 1 ms and the database in about 50 ms. 90 of 100 reads are cache hits. Which result matters more?
options: The average read drops to about 6 ms
The cache never has old data
The database sees 10 questions instead of 100, which is 10 times less load
Every user gets the same answer faster than 1 ms
why: Both numbers are true, but the database is the hardest part to make bigger, so the load number matters more. A cache mainly protects the database.

q: The price of a product changes. With cache aside, what should the app do on the write?
options: Change the database, then delete the cached copy
Change the database, then write the new price into the cache
Change only the cache and let the database catch up
Change only the database and wait for the cache to notice
why: Delete, do not overwrite. Two writers can finish in the wrong order, and then the older value wins in the cache. A delete has no value to get wrong, and the next read fills the cache with the truth.

q: A copy has a TTL of 10 minutes. A script changes the price in the database and does not delete the copy. How old can the price a user sees be, at worst?
options: Zero, a TTL always makes the copy fresh
About 1 minute
About 5 minutes
Up to 10 minutes
why: The TTL does not make a copy fresh. It only limits how long a copy can stay old. Always set a TTL, even when you delete on write, as the backup for a missed delete.

q: A very busy copy ends at 12:00:00 and 1,000 requests miss in the same second. The database slows down, users press reload, and it gets worse. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the TTL on every key to one year
Let the first miss refill the copy and make the others wait for that one refill, or refresh the copy before it ends
Turn off the cache so the database is used directly
Give each request its own copy of the key
why: A stampede is many equal misses at once. In the lesson run, 5 requests with no protection made 5 database calls, and with one shared refill only 1.

q: The code deletes the cached copy first and then changes the database. Users still see the old price for 10 minutes. What happened?
options: The TTL was too short
Redis did not delete the key
The delete ran twice
A reader missed in the gap, read the old price from the database and saved it as a new copy, and nothing deleted it again
why: Delete after the change is saved, not before. Deleting first leaves a gap where a reader can refill the cache with the old row. A rare race can still happen after the right order, and the TTL limits it.

q: A payment page shows your balance, and the team wants to cache it for 5 minutes. What is the best answer?
options: No. A balance used to decide about money is read from the database, because an old copy could let someone pay with money they no longer have
Yes, 5 minutes is short enough for money
Yes, but only on the first read of the day
Yes, if the key includes the word balance
why: Cache answers that are asked again and again, change rarely and may be a few seconds old, like a product list. Do not cache what decides about money or stock, and never cache secrets.
